topic: Build-cost vs use-cost trade-off of a network design
idea: Score a network by total road length (least cost to build) against mean route detour/travel cost between boundary pairs (least cost to use); the complete graph is the user-optimal extreme, the spanning tree the build-optimal one, real networks sit between (4-node example: 60 km vs 20 km vs hybrid 30 km).
does: Reports total length, the length of the minimum spanning tree and complete-graph lower/upper bounds, and mean detour ratio, so a design lies on a build-cost to use-cost scale; useful for comparing scenarios in run_experiment.
outputs: total length km, MST length, ratio to MST, mean detour index, position on scale 0..1
notes: Pure graph computation, stdlib only. Spanning-tree length via Kruskal.

idea: Same disruption hurts differently by node type: hub-and-spoke is efficient but loses connectivity when the hub fails; mesh networks degrade gracefully. Classify network by degree distribution (regular, small-world, scale-free via few high-degree vertices) and report hub dependence.
does: Degree-distribution class plus the share of OD pairs disconnected or detoured by removing each top-degree junction, relating to hub dependence; extends critical_links to junctions and the topology class.
outputs: class label (regular/scale-free-like), per-junction removal impact on reachable pairs and mean detour
notes: Junction-removal variant of critical_links is the new part.

idea: Demand responds to cost: elasticity e (e.g. -0.5 for vehicle use against operating cost; commuting inelastic in money but elastic in time) so demand at new cost = demand * (cost1/cost0)^e. Added capacity lowers time, which induces mode, route, time-of-day shifts and new trips until supply and demand meet at an equilibrium (Fig 3.11). Iterate run -> mean OD travel time -> rescale OD -> run.
does: Runs a scenario, reads mean travel time per OD pair, rescales each pair's demand by the time-elasticity, repeats until demand changes under a tolerance; reports induced trips and the equilibrium time, so a capacity upgrade is not judged on fixed demand.
inputs: elasticity per pair or global, tolerance, max iterations, scenario
outputs: equilibrium OD matrix, induced demand %, time before and after, iterations
existing: partial: scale_demand, calibrate_demand, choose_modes (all fixed demand; not_built says test demand is fixed before scenarios)
notes: Elasticity -0.5 is the book's example; the demand-time damping avoids oscillation (use method of successive averages).

topic: Service quality dimensions for scheduled services
idea: Break a service's time quality into transport time, timing, punctuality (mean deviation from schedule) and frequency (departures per period); high frequency ties up vehicles (asset utilisation).
does: Report for each bus line mean headway, headway variability, schedule deviation (punctuality) and load factor from a run.
notes: Generic; only worthwhile if bus delay KPIs are not already reported.

idea: Each mode has cost = fixed (terminal / access / waiting) + variable per km; the cheaper mode switches at a break-even distance D = (F2-F1)/(v1-v2). Apply to travel time: bus/walk/car door-to-door time against trip length gives the distance where a mode wins, explaining choose_modes splits.
does: For each OD pair compute door-to-door time per vehicle type (access/wait fixed part plus distance/speed) and report the crossover distance and which pairs lie each side, as a sanity check or input for choose_modes.
inputs: vehicle types (speed, access/wait time), OD distances
outputs: break-even distance per type pair, dominant mode per OD pair
notes: Linear cost structure only; book stresses real networks deviate.

idea: About half of urban congestion is recurrent (demand peaks at set times and places) and half non-recurrent (accidents, weather, events, linked to incident response). Decompose delay across seeds: the cross-seed mean delay per link and time bin is recurrent; the cross-seed excess variance or the tail above it is non-recurrent.
does: From a multi-seed experiment (or batch with incidents or emergency vehicles) splits total vehicle delay per link and time bin into a recurrent part (median across seeds) and a non-recurrent part (excess over the median), and ranks links by each, so design fixes (capacity) are separated from incident management fixes.
inputs: experiment id with several seeds (per-link delay or speed series)
outputs: recurrent share %, non-recurrent share %, top links of each, time bins
notes: Needs per-link per-bin series saved by each run; 'half is recurrent' is a book rule of thumb, not a parameter.

idea: A sudden brake makes the bottleneck move upstream (backward-travelling wave) and the stop location is not the cause; congestion can end in total immobilisation. Detect from detector speed series: onset time per detector and the upstream propagation speed.
does: Finds when each successive upstream detector drops below a speed threshold, fits the backward wave speed (km/h) and origin link, and reports whether a jam started at a junction, a bus stop, an emergency vehicle or a lane change, helping the assistant diagnose causes.
inputs: detector series of a run, speed threshold
outputs: events: origin link, start time, wave speed, extent, duration
existing: partial: read_detectors, analyse_run (queues); none for wave tracing
notes: Book gives no formula; standard kinematic-wave reading gives wave speed = dx/dt between onsets.

idea: Sanity-check generated demand against rules of thumb: 3-4 trips per resident per day, about 1 to 1.2 hours per day of travel time (constant travel-time budget), locations within 5 minutes walk are pedestrian, mode share priors by city type (transit 25-50% in dense Asian/European cores, car 89% Dallas, cycling 38% Amsterdam).
does: Compares institutions people, trips per person, mean OD travel time per day and mode shares with these benchmarks and warns on outliers, before a run.
inputs: institutions, OD matrix, mode shares, run mean trip times
outputs: table: metric, value, benchmark range, flag
cite: Ch 8 Concept 3, Trip generation, Modal split
notes: Benchmarks are broad; flag, never refuse.

idea: Resilience = capability to resume operations at the pre-disruption level; the smaller the drop in capacity and fluidity and the faster the recovery, the higher it is. Close a road or lane for a window mid-run, track a performance series (mean speed, throughput, queue) and report the drop, recovery time and the area lost (resilience triangle); the vulnerability is dynamic, not free-flow.
does: Runs a baseline and a seed-paired disrupted run (road/lane closed for a given window, or an emergency vehicle stopped), then reports max performance drop, time to recover to 95% of baseline, delay area (veh-h) and a resilience index (1 - lost area / baseline area); can be looped over critical_links candidates to rank by dynamic impact.
inputs: road/lane to close, start and end time, performance metric, seeds
outputs: drop %, recovery time s, lost vehicle-hours, resilience index, paired t-test across seeds
existing: partial: critical_links (static, free flow); run_experiment (scenarios static)
notes: Needs a timed closure event in the simulation (not a permanent edit); flexibility = alternative routes, redundancy = parallel paths, both from network_indices.

idea: Congestion pricing: a cordon charge to enter the centre or a lane whose toll rises as speed falls (free when flowing). Treat the toll as a generalised-cost term in route and mode choice; compare the pricing scenario against baseline with run_experiment.
does: Adds a toll in money to chosen roads, a cordon set, or a managed lane, converts it with a value of time to seconds in route choice and mode choice, and optionally makes it dynamic (toll proportional to the congestion level) so the assistant can test pricing designs.
inputs: roads or cordon, toll, value of time, dynamic rule
outputs: changed route/mode splits, revenue, delay change
cite: Ch 9 Concept 2, Transport demand management and pricing
notes: Book gives examples (London 2003, Stockholm, Singapore) not parameters; needs value of time as input; interacts with the elastic-demand idea.

topic: Extended graph indices: cost_rel, pi, eta, theta, transitivity, hierarchy
idea: Add the indices network_indices lacks: Cost = sum aij*lij and Cost_rel = (Cost - Cost_MST)/(Cost_GT - Cost_MST) with MST by Kruskal and GT the greedy triangulation (0 least efficient, 1 near optimal); network density ND = L/S (km per km2); Pi = L(G)/D(diameter); Eta = L(G)/e (mean link length); Theta = Q(G)/v (mean traffic load per node, or per link); transitivity (closed triplets over possible triplets, Ci = lambda/tau); hierarchy exponent h from a log-log fit of node frequency against degree; Koenig number (eccentricity) per node.
does: Extra fields in network_indices so designs can be compared on spatial efficiency, density and clustering, with theta turning run flows into load per link.
inputs: network geometry (metres), optionally a run's link flows
outputs: cost_rel, density km/km2, pi, eta, theta, transitivity, hierarchy exponent, eccentricity per junction
existing: partial: network_indices (alpha, beta, gamma, diameter, degrees, detour, Shimbel); covered: Gini flow concentration (stats.gini)
cite: Appendix Method 3, Cost/Cost_rel, ND, Pi, Eta, Theta, Hierarchy, Transitivity
notes: Greedy triangulation: add all non-crossing shortest candidate edges in length order; stdlib only. Theta needs flows so best on run results.

idea: An articulation node is a junction whose removal disconnects the graph; an isthmus is a road whose removal splits the network in two (it also reveals dense communities when removed repeatedly). Find by depth-first lowpoint search in O(V+E) as a topological single-point-of-failure list.
does: Lists articulation junctions and bridge roads (with which junctions or boundary ends each cut isolates), complementing critical_links which ranks by traffic loss; cheap check before editing or running a disruption test.
inputs: network graph (directed use for one-way roads: strongly connected check)
outputs: articulation junctions, bridge roads, size of the cut-off part and its boundary ends
existing: partial: analyse_network (disconnected parts, unreachable junctions); critical_links (traffic-weighted vulnerability)
notes: Also gives nodal regions (single-linkage by removing weaker links) and communities for grouping signal coordination.

topic: Potential and isochrone accessibility of places
idea: Potential accessibility A_i = sum_j P_j / d_ij (Hansen type) with P_j an attribute (people, employees, retail), d_ij the shortest-path time; row sums give emissiveness, column sums attractiveness (matrix not symmetric); geographic accessibility A(G)_i = sum_j d_ij / n (lower = better); contiguous/isochrone accessibility counts opportunities reachable within T minutes; total accessibility T = sum_{k=1..D} C^k counts direct and indirect paths.
does: Computes, per junction and institution, geographic accessibility, potential accessibility weighted by institution people and employees (travel times from free flow or from a run's measured link times), jobs reachable within 15/30 min, plus an equity Gini of accessibility across places; compares design variants (a new road's gain in accessibility) and flags poorly served institutions.
inputs: network, institutions (people, employees), travel-time matrix (free flow or run), time thresholds
outputs: per-place geographic and potential accessibility, emissiveness, attractiveness, opportunities within T, Gini of accessibility, change between scenarios
existing: partial: network_indices (Shimbel accessibility on topology only); critical_links
cite: Appendix Method 5, Geographic and potential accessibility, A(G), A(P), total accessibility T
notes: The book writes A(P)=sum Pi + sum Pj/dij; use the Hansen form sum Pj/dij (distance deterrence could be exp(-beta d) to match the gravity model already used by generate_demand). Inputs already exist in the app: institutions' people/employees.

topic: Fundamental diagram per link: capacity, critical density and speed
idea: Capacity is the maximal hourly flow; critical density and critical speed are those at which volume is maximal; density = volume/speed (1000 veh/h at 50 km/h gives 20 veh/km). Reference capacities 1000 veh/lane/h continuous and 500 veh/lane/h discontinuous. Fit a flow-density curve from detector data and report observed capacity, critical density/speed, and the load factor (flow over capacity).
does: From read_detectors series builds the flow-density-speed scatter per link, estimates observed capacity (high percentile flow), critical density and speed, and flags links whose peak load factor nears 1; compares with the quoted lane capacity as a calibration of Krauss parameters.
outputs: capacity veh/h, critical density veh/km, critical speed km/h, load factor per link, outliers
existing: partial: read_detectors (density, counts, speeds per link), check_calibration (flows only)
notes: No formula beyond definitions; fitting could use a triangular fundamental diagram by least squares.

idea: Performance is a ratio, interpreted only comparatively across space or time: mean distance travelled, mean trips per capita, utilisation coefficient (time used over time available), load factor, punctuality, reliability, speed/turnover.
does: Adds to run summaries mean trip length, trips per person, vehicle utilisation (share of time moving) and bus load factor and punctuality, shown beside a comparison run.

idea: The retail model sets the market boundary between two locations by their separation weighted by relative importance: B_ij = d_ij / (1 + sqrt(W_j / W_i)) from i (Reilly's law of retail gravitation); equal weights give the midpoint. Use it to cut the overlapping circles of influence of institutions into non-overlapping catchments so shared origins go to the stronger or nearer institution.
does: Computes pairwise breaking points between institutions (by people/employees as weight, road distance) and assigns each origin junction/end to one institution (or splits it by gravity weights) rather than equal shares across overlapping catchments; reports each institution's resulting catchment people.
inputs: institutions (centre, people, employees), junctions and ends with road distances
outputs: breaking point per pair, catchment assignment, catchment people per institution
existing: partial: list_institutions (circle of influence with equal shares; not_built says catchment places not weighted by distance or population)
cite: Appendix Method 8, Retail model, Fig A.30
notes: Book gives the principle and a worked example (boundary 4.9 from i, 2.1 from j at distance 7) but not the equation; the square-root form is standard Reilly.

topic: Gravity model with separate emissivity, attractiveness and friction exponents, and intervening opportunities
idea: Tij = k Pi^lambda Pj^alpha / dij^beta: beta friction (lower on highways, falls as transport improves), lambda emissivity, alpha attractiveness; calibrate by matching observed flows. Three conditions must hold for an interaction: complementarity, lack of intervening opportunity (a closer equivalent destination takes the trip), transferability (cost below benefit). Destination-choice models add income, walkability, parking.
does: Fits k, lambda, alpha, beta of the gravity model to counts or an observed OD matrix (log-linear regression, or Poisson fit), tests the intervening-opportunity variant (rank destinations by distance and discount trips by opportunities nearer than j), and reports goodness of fit; generate_demand can then use the fitted exponents.
inputs: observed OD matrix or counted flows, origin and destination attributes, distances
outputs: k, lambda, alpha, beta with standard errors, R2, RMSE, intervening-opportunity variant fit
existing: partial: generate_demand (gravity, Furness), calibrate_demand (counts); not_built lists power-law deterrence and Poisson ML gravity calibration from an observed matrix
cite: Appendix Method 8, gravity model with alpha, lambda, beta; conditions for spatial flows
notes: Log-linearising Tij gives OLS on ln Pi, ln Pj, ln dij using the existing regress tool; zero cells need handling.
